anchoring: Fixating on a reference number, such as your purchase price, when judging what to do now.
ask: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept. Market buys fill near the ask.
backtest: Running a trading rule on historical data to see how it would have done.
benchmark: A simple alternative, such as buying a broad index fund and holding it, used to judge whether active decisions added value.
bid: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay. Market sells fill near the bid.
commission: A fee charged by the broker for each order. This game uses a flat $0.99 per order by default.
confirmation bias: Seeking out information that supports what you already believe and discounting what contradicts it.
correlation: How closely two investments move together. Highly correlated holdings diversify each other less.
crossover: When a shorter moving average crosses above or below a longer one, often used as a trend signal.
disposition effect: The tendency to sell winning investments too early and hold losing ones too long.
diversification: Spreading money across investments that do not all move together, so one bad outcome hurts less.
dividend: A cash payment from a company to its shareholders.
drawdown: The fall in value from a previous peak to a later low, usually shown as a percentage.
etf: Exchange-traded fund: a basket of many securities that trades like a single stock. VT, for example, holds thousands of companies worldwide.
ex-dividend date: The first day a share trades without the right to the upcoming dividend. You must own it before this date.
fx spread: The cost of converting one currency into another, here SGD to USD, built into the exchange rate you get.
in-sample: The part of the data used to choose or tune a strategy. Results here are optimistic.
lookahead bias: Accidentally using information in a test that would not have been available at the time.
loss aversion: Losses feel more painful than equal-sized gains feel good, which makes people avoid realising losses.
loss limit: A pre-set loss (here 15% below your average cost) at which you re-examine a position. This game alerts you but never sells for you.
market order: An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price, accepting whatever fill you get.
maximum drawdown: The largest peak-to-trough fall over a period: a measure of the worst stretch you would have lived through.
moving average: The average closing price over the last N trading days, recalculated daily. It smooths out noise but lags.
out-of-sample: Data not used to choose a strategy, used to test it more honestly.
overconfidence: Overrating your own skill or information, often leading to trading too much.
overfitting: Tuning a strategy so closely to past data that it captures noise and fails on new data.
position sizing: Deciding how much money to put into a single position.
recency bias: Giving too much weight to recent events and assuming they will continue.
resulting: Judging the quality of a decision only by its outcome, ignoring luck.
round trip: Buying and later selling the same position, paying trading costs on both sides.
slippage: The difference between the expected price and the price you actually get, caused by price movement and order size.
spread: The gap between the bid and the ask. Trading immediately costs you roughly half of it on each side.
stock split: Dividing each share into several, for example 4-for-1. The share count rises, the price falls, and the value stays the same.
stop-loss order: An order that becomes a market order when the price falls to a set level. A gap can fill it well below that level.
survivorship bias: Studying only the winners that still exist, which makes past results look better than they were.
total return: Price change plus dividends received: the full return of an investment.
volatility: How much and how quickly a price moves up and down.
walk-forward: Choosing strategy settings on earlier data, then testing them unchanged on later data.
whipsaw: Being pushed in and out of a position by short-term noise, paying costs each time.
withholding tax: Tax deducted at source. The US withholds 30% of dividends paid to many non-US investors.
